title: KV-cache shard skew and quantization interaction: investigation, mitigation, and runbook
author: Marco Delgado
body:
Summary:
This document captures an investigation into a recurring class of production incidents where uneven KV-cache (prefix/KV) distribution across shard workers combined with aggressive post-training quantization (8-bit asymmetric) produced high tail latency and occasional OOMs. It includes root-cause evidence, detection queries, a short-term mitigation runbook, recommended scheduler and quantization configuration changes, and a checklist for long-term fixes and testing.

Scope and impact:
- Affects: hosted and dedicated serving pools using split-shard KV routing + quantized model families (q8_a and q8_b).
- Symptom window: intermittent p99/p999 spikes (200–800ms over baseline), spikes concentrated during synthetic-batched workloads and long-context chat sessions (>= 2048 tokens).
- Frequency: 3 incidents between 2025-09 and 2025-11 in US-east-1 GPU pools; reproduction locally with shard skew simulator.
- Business impact: API error rate increased 1.4–2.3x during events; customers on Dedicated saw throughput degradation prompting support escalations.

Key findings (short form):
1) Shard assignment heuristic allowed up to 2.5x more active KV-entries on certain workers for common long-prefix prompts, causing memory pressure and slower KV lookups.
2) Quantized kernels (8-bit asymmetric) for recent model variants introduce nonuniform per-layer memory layout that increases temporary workspace allocation variance per token. When combined with prefetching, this exacerbated peak memory use.
3) Kernel scheduler prioritized throughput over memory headroom during steady-state autoscaling; under high skew this led to transient OOM kills and a cascade of request retries that amplified tail latencies.

Relevant metrics and alerting thresholds:
- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard (gauge) — alert if max_shard / median_shard > 1.6 for 5m
- kv_cache_hit_rate (percent) — warn if < 92% for 10m on a model route
- gpu_mem_headroom_pct (gauge) — critical if any device < 12% for 1m
- request_latency_ms{route} p99 and p999 — critical if p999 > baseline_p999 * 3 for 5m
- kernel_scheduler_pending_queue_length — warn if > 1000 for 2m

PromQL examples (Grafana):
- Shard skew ratio:
  max(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"}) / avg(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"})
- GPU headroom percentage (device-level):
  100 * (1 - (avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_used_bytes[1m]) / avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_total_bytes[1m])))

Investigation artifacts (evidence):
- Kernel traces showing repeated cudaMalloc failure -> fallback path for q8 kernels (attached as trace IDs: trc-20251004-42, trc-20251021-08).
- Heap dumps from affected workers demonstrating 60–80% of incremental allocations were temporary layer workspaces tied to the quantized fused-kernel (dump ids: heap-20251004-a, heap-20251102-b).
- Repro script: scripts/kv-skew-sim/runner.py (internal repo: infra/sim) — reproduces p99 spike by driving long-prefix variety and forcing unbalanced shard assignment.

Immediate mitigation (short-term runbook) — use during incidents:
1) Detect: confirm shard_skew_ratio PromQL > 1.6 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct any device < 12% or p999 > baseline*2.
2) Quarantine affected model route: add a temp-route override to route requests to a non-quantized fallback model (e.g., model-xv2-fp16) via the routing control plane.
3) Throttle synthetic-heavy customers: apply per-client rate limit for 10m windows on routes causing skew.
4) Rebalance shards: trigger targeted shard-respin for the worker pool (CLI):
   - rcli shard rebalance --pool us-east-1-prod --strategy uniform --drain=true --concurrency=2
5) If OOM persists, scale up a hotfix worker-sized pool with higher-memory instances:
   - terraform: apply -var='pool_size=4' -target=module.hotfix-us-east1
6) Monitor: ensure kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard ratio returns < 1.2 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct > 18% before resuming normal routing.

Commands and ops snippets:
- Check shard skew quickly (kubectl + prom):
  kubectl -n serving exec -it svc/prom-query -- curl -sG 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query' --data-urlencode 'query=max(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"}) / avg(kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard{pool="us-east-1-prod"})' | jq
- Force scheduler to prefer memory headroom (onbox flag):
  echo 'MEMORY_FIRST=1' > /etc/redwood/runtime_flags.d/priority.conf && systemctl restart redwood-runtime-scheduler.service

Root-cause analysis (detailed):
- Allocation pattern: the quantized fused attention kernel uses dynamic temporaries sized to sequence length and per-layer hidden-size alignment. Some hardware-specific kernel variants pad workspace to 64-byte boundaries; combined with our allocator metadata this produced a 20–40% bloat versus FP16 kernels under long sequences.
- Shard topology and assignment: the greedy prefix hash used for low-latency routing did not incorporate current KV cache size or recent allocation footprint. That optimization favored route-affinity but ignored memory balance.
- Scheduler policy: the priority-driven scheduler groups tasks into batches by estimated token cost but uses static headroom thresholds. In skewed scenarios it allowed many high-cost requests to land on a single worker because affinity minimization lowered request hop cost metric.

Design decisions and trade-offs considered:
- Option A — Always prefer FP16 fallback for long-context (>2048) requests: reduces cost/throughput but increases latency per token slightly for some model families.
- Option B — Update shard assignment to be headroom-aware: requires global KV size propagation (adds 200–400ms route lookup overhead unless cached).
- Option C — Kernel change: adjust quantized kernels to pre-reserve workspace conservatively, reducing dynamic allocation churn (engineering cost high, long lead time).
Recommendation: Combine B + short-term A during rollout. B provides the most sustainable operational improvement with tolerable lookup overhead if we cache single-key headroom info in the routing plane.

Planned short-to-medium term fixes (owners and ETA):
- Immediate (SRE / eng-serving-runtime) — Implement a headroom-aware shard assignment flag and enable in canary pool (owner: Ravi Patel) — ETA: 2026-03-10.
- Near-term (runtime team) — Add memory-first scheduler mode toggles and expose on control-plane flags (owner: Aisha Kumar) — ETA: 2026-04-01.
- Medium (kernel team) — Rework q8 fused-kernel workspace allocation to use pooled temporaries and deterministic preallocation (owner: Lena Schwartz) — ETA: 2026-07-15.

Testing and benchmarking plan (how we will validate):
1) Add a new scenario to the perf-suite: long-context mixed-prefix workload with intentional skew (workload id: long-prefix-skew-2026). Benchmarks: p50/p95/p99/p999 latency, tokens/sec, retry rate, GPU util, mem headroom.
2) Unit tests for shard assignment: simulate 10k concurrent prefixes and assert skew ratio < 1.3 under headroom-aware policy.
3) Kernel perf run: compare q8_old vs q8_pooled on sequence lengths 512/1024/2048 measuring workspace allocations (nvprof traces).
4) Canary rollout: enable headroom-aware routing in dedicated canary pool of 5 workers for 72h; if p999 regressions occur > 10% abort.

Acceptance criteria for rollout:
- Canary p999 latency does not increase by more than 10% relative to baseline for the same traffic mix.
- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard ratio <= 1.3 sustained for 24h.
- No device reports gpu_mem_headroom_pct < 10% for more than 1 minute.

Operational notes and playbook tips:
- When rebalancing, prefer graceful drain (drain=true) to avoid losing KV in-flight; allow 60s for KV transfer per shard.
- Avoid enabling both memory-first scheduler and aggressive batching in the same pool simultaneously—conflicting objectives can hurt throughput.
- Document temporary route fallbacks in the routing change log with the incident tag (inc-20251004-kv-skew).

Developer checklist for implementations:
- Add integration tests in infra/sim for skewed KV distributions and quantized kernel stress.
- Add end-to-end benchmark in perf-suite with automated alerting hook comparing new runs to historical baselines.
- Update the Runtime Scheduler config schema (runtime-configs/scheduler_v2.yaml):
  # example excerpt
  scheduler_mode: \"memory_first|throughput_first\"
  memory_headroom_threshold_pct: 18
  shard_assignment_cache_ttl_ms: 250
  headroom_propagation: true

Change log (brief):
- 2026-02-18: Published doc and runbook; added PromQL detection query and immediate mitigation steps.
- 2025-11-12: Initial post-incident analysis draft created.

Related resources:
- perf-suite workload definitions: infra/perf/long-prefix-skew-2026.yaml
- Kernel trace bundle: s3://redwood-internal/traces/kv-skew-q8-2025/
- Simulation runner: git@internal:redwood/infra/sim.git (branch: kv-skew-fixes)

Appendix A — Example alert runbook (short):
1) Pager triggers: SRE oncall receives p999 alert for route X.
2) Triage: confirm shard_skew_ratio > 1.6 and check pool memory headroom.
3) Action: apply temporary route override to FP16 fallback and trigger shard rebalance.
4) Post-incident: run heap-dump collector on affected workers and upload to s3 with tag inc-YYYYMMDD-kvskew.

Appendix B — Experimental notes from local reproducer:
- On an AWS p4d-like instance: sequence length 4096 + q8 kernel -> temporary allocations peaked at 64MB per layer; reducing per-layer workspace alignment to 32 bytes reduced peak by ~18%.

Owner contact and escalation:
- Primary owner: Marco Delgado <marco@redwood.ai>
- SRE escalation: oncall@redwood.ai (pager duty)

If you make changes to scheduler flags or shard assignment heuristics, add a short design note in eng-serving-runtime/decision-records and tag reviewers: Aisha Kumar, Lena Schwartz, Ravi Patel.
